identification.summary: Russian military intelligence (GRU Unit 26165) cyber actor focused on strategic intelligence targets [S1]. Since 2022 it has focused on Ukraine's war effort and on Western logistics and technology companies that coordinate and deliver aid to Ukraine, including compromising IP cameras at border crossings to track shipments [S2]. It uses custom tools such as GooseEgg alongside public exploits [S1].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2004 [S3]. GooseEgg in use since at least June 2020, possibly April 2019 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Forest Blizzard (formerly STRONTIUM). Microsoft maps FANCY BEAR, APT28, Sofacy, Sednit and others to it [S5]; MITRE tracks it as APT28 (G0007) [S3]. Nineteen APT29 names that the source merge had placed on this record (e.g. Cozy Bear, NOBELIUM, Dark Halo) were moved to Midnight Blizzard.

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation: GRU 85th Main Special Service Center (GTsSS), military Unit 26165 [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: US and UK governments attribute the actor to GRU Unit 26165 [S1]. A multinational joint advisory (21 May 2025) attributes the logistics-targeting campaign to Unit 26165 [S2].
attribution.basis: Government attribution and joint advisory [S2]; Microsoft telemetry and malware analysis [S1].

objectives: Strategic intelligence for the Russian military and state. Since 2022, collection on Ukraine and on the Western logistics and technology firms that move aid to Ukraine, including tracking shipments through compromised cameras, which agencies assess could enable sabotage or kinetic targeting [S2].

sectors: IP cameras at Ukrainian border crossings and in Ukraine and bordering NATO states
regions: NATO member states, Western Europe and North America
targeting.notes: Sector targeting from Microsoft [S1] and the 2025 joint advisory as summarized by the German BfV and coverage [S2][S4].

capabilities.summary: Credential theft and privilege escalation with GooseEgg, which exploits Windows Print Spooler CVE-2022-38028 [S1]. Public exploits, including CVE-2023-23397 [S1]. In the 2025 campaign: password spraying, spear-phishing and modification of Exchange mailbox permissions to maintain access [S2][S4]. Compromise of internet-connected IP cameras for surveillance [S2]. MITRE lists 93 techniques and 29 software entries, including X-Agent (CHOPSTICK), Zebrocy, LoJax, Drovorub and LAMEHUG [S3].

campaigns.name: GooseEgg / Print Spooler exploitation
campaigns.summary: Custom tool exploiting CVE-2022-38028 against Ukrainian, Western European and North American government, NGO, education and transportation organizations. Used since at least June 2020.

campaigns.name: Targeting Western logistics and technology firms
campaigns.summary: Campaign against organizations coordinating, transporting and delivering aid to Ukraine, plus wide-scale IP camera targeting in Ukraine and bordering NATO nations. Joint advisory published 21 May 2025.

diamond.capability: GooseEgg; public exploits (CVE-2023-23397, CVE-2022-38028); password spraying; spear-phishing; Exchange mailbox permission abuse; X-Agent, Zebrocy, LoJax and related families [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled and compromised infrastructure for phishing and C2; compromised IP cameras used as collection sensors [S2].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian and Western government, defense, logistics, transportation, IT and education organizations [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Military intelligence support to Russia's war in Ukraine, especially visibility into Western aid flows [S2].
diamond.technology: Weak authentication on mail systems and widespread, poorly secured IoT cameras [S2].

gaps: Primary text of the 21 May 2025 joint advisory (AA25-141A) could not be fetched (CISA and BSI blocked); verify CVE list, camera counts and named countries against the PDF.
Earlier landmark events (2016 DNC intrusion and the 2018 DOJ indictment of GRU officers, Drovorub advisory, Ubiquiti EdgeRouter disruption in 2024) are not yet sourced in this profile.
Whether camera-derived intelligence has been used to cue physical sabotage or strikes is an agency assessment, not a confirmed event.
Some remaining aliases (e.g. Grizzly Steppe, which named joint APT28/APT29 activity) are ambiguous.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The cyberspace OE includes commercial logistics providers, rail and port operators, and the IoT cameras along supply routes into Ukraine and NATO's eastern flank. These are intelligence collection points for the adversary. STEP 2: Compromised cameras turn the physical terrain itself into adversary ISR, which affects OPSEC for movements. STEP 3: The template is password spraying or phishing against mail accounts, then mailbox permission changes for persistence, then collection on shipments and schedules. In parallel, mass compromise of exposed cameras. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection on aid logistics to inform Russian targeting and diplomacy. MDCOA is using collected movement data to cue sabotage or strikes on aid shipments or nodes. Candidate indicators: new mailbox delegation or folder permissions, spray activity against logistics firms, and anomalous access to camera management interfaces near routes [S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Treat commercial partners' camera and mail exposure as part of force-protection planning for movements. (2) JCC2 situational awareness should take in partner and industry reporting on logistics-sector intrusions, since the victims are mostly private. (3) Authorities: hardening of commercial and allied camera networks is a partner-nation and owner responsibility. DoD influence is through contracts, requirements and liaison. (4) OPSEC: plan movement security assuming adversary visibility through compromised cameras on routes.
